newsitem.title: UK: N.Ireland Orange Order parades after violence.
newsitem.headline: N.Ireland Orange Order parades after violence.

text.p: Suspected Republican gunmen shot and wounded five security personnel and two teenage Protestants overnight as Northern Ireland's Orange Order marched in thousands to mark the most hallowed date in its calendar.

The head of Northern Ireland's biggest political group, the pro-British Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), accused the Irish Republican Army (IRA) and its political arm, Sinn Fein, of responsibility for the violence.
"It just underlines the evil intent of Sinn Fein/IRA," David Trimble told the BBC.
Sinn Fein, which seeks an end to British rule in Northern Ireland, had campaigned for many of Saturday's marches to be scrapped as a concession to the minority Catholic population.

On Friday the Orange Order called off four of hundreds of Saturday's parades under threat of mass Catholic protest and security fears after a week of violence sparked by a march down a Catholic part of rural Portadown last Sunday.
British Prime Minister Tony Blair urged Sinn Fein to respond to the Orange Order's move by getting the IRA to declare the ceasefire that would admit it to peace talks.
"In the last two days, the Orange Order by their decision have opted for hope. I congratulate them. Sinn Fein can now respond," he told a youth conference in Britain.

Sinn Fein is barred from Northern Ireland peace talks since the IRA ended a 17-month truce in February last year and resumed its war against British rule of the province. The Order scrapped marches in Belfast, Newry, Armagh and rerouted another parade in Londonderry in a landmark decision that ended decades of stubborn refusal to accept objections by Catholics who see such demonstrations as intimidation .
On Saturday the Order also called off a parade in Dunloy, 50 miles (80 km) north of Belfast because of a protest by 200 Catholic nationalists and another march in Bellaghy.
But elsewhere the Orange Order, founded to celebrate its Protestant faith and British Loyalty, staged hundreds of parades which were to converge into about 20 big marches.

Behind pipe bands and drums, members of the 80,000 strong Orange Order paraded in Belfast watched by thousands of Protestants who lined the streets from early in the morning to take part in what is supposed to be a yearly family carnival.
The Orange Order decision had raised hopes that this year's "Glorious 12th of July" parades would pass off peacefully.

But republican gunmen were out on the steets late on Friday night and injured three soldiers and two police in a carefully planned ambush in North Belfast. They fired about 20 shots at the joint patrol and hurled what was believed to be a "pipe bomb," a crude home-made device, injuring the patrol just before Protestants lit bonfires across the province on the eve of their July 12 anniversary.
Cecil Walker, a Belfast member of parliament for the UUP, said the attack was a bitter disappointment after the Orange Order's decision to cancel its parades.
"There are obviously elements in the nationalist community who seem to be holding on to mayhem."
The teenagers, one aged 14 and the other 18, were hurt in shootings early on Saturday as they attended a Belfast bonfire, one of hundreds which burned across the province until dawn.
Security forces said a mortar was fired at a British army helicopter pad in the staunchly Irish nationalist county of Armagh on the border with Ireland but no-one was hurt.
Saturday's festivities commemorate a 1690 Protestant victory over Catholic forces at the Battle of the Boyne which ensured that a Protestant ascended the British throne.
